evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; character entry 喜
evidence.text: The database reports oracle-bone and bronze forms with 壴 and 口. It interprets 壴 as an early drum graph and proposes that the compound conveys making music by beating a drum and singing, hence joy. This is a scholarly analysis, not a directly observable meaning of the shapes.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 喜

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; entry 喜, cited oracle-bone and bronze usages
evidence.text: It cites oracle-bone examples 《合集》15671「王其喜」 and 《合集》21207「不喜」, analyzing them as joy/rejoicing, alongside uses as personal and polity names. It reports bronze uses as names, music terminology, joy (including 井弔鐘「用喜樂文神人」), and a ritual use in 天亡簋「事喜(饎)上帝」. The latter is a distinct reading/use and does not by itself establish a semantic development from joy to sacrifice. The page gives inscription identifiers but no absolute dates for these examples.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 喜

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; entry 壴
evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone and bronze 壴 as depicting an upright drum, with a top ornament, drum face, and support; it calls 壴 an early graph for 鼓, and notes independent uses for striking a drum and musical terminology. This supports the component's semantic identification as a drum graph. It does not establish 壴 as a phonetic in 喜.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 壴

evidence.source: 中央研究院漢字構形資料庫 (Academia Sinica Character Database)
evidence.text: The page lists graphic categories for oracle-bone, bronze (including inscription index 集成04137), Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen forms. Its explanation identifies upper 壴 as an ancient Chinese drum and lower 口, and offers two interpretive possibilities: hearing drum music and smiling, or placing the drum on its stand to signal a celebratory event requiring music. These are alternative interpretations, not a demonstrated chronology of senses.
evidence.title: 漢字「喜」：字形演變

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A00628, research notes for 喜 and variants 憙, 歖
evidence.text: The dictionary reproduces the Shuowen explanation「喜，樂也。從壴從口」and the separate Shuowen entry 憙「說也。從心從喜，喜亦聲」. It notes that 憙 was later sometimes conflated with 喜, while citing an analysis distinguishing joy from liking/desire. It reports 歖 as a Shuowen 'ancient form' of 喜, described there as formed with 欠. The web page further discusses later scribal variants and cautions that one variant's altered top is a writing convenience/corruption rather than evidence about the original graph.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

Opened character-specific entry and verified component analysis, traditional gloss, cited oracle-bone and bronze examples, and 壴’s independent drum-related evidence.

gaps: The source pages identify script classes and an inscription index, but no visually inspected glyph image was used, and no dated palaeographic witness with a secure absolute date was established here. The oracle-bone and bronze examples are reported through a modern database, which supplies corpus identifiers rather than dates.

The early uses of 喜 include personal/polity-name uses, joy readings, and a reported ritual reading 喜(饎). Their chronological ordering and the semantic relationship between the ritual reading and ordinary joy are not established by inspected evidence.

The graph's component analysis is disputed at the level of intended motivation: modern databases describe a semantic compound (drum/music plus mouth/singing), while a meeting note found in search results reports scholarly disagreement over whether some unaccompanied 壴 shapes represent 喜 and whether the graph can have multiple readings. The paper containing the fuller discussion was inaccessible; no sound-component analysis is established here.

No verified kMandarin row for 壴 was obtained, and the supplied primary-reading packet provides no 壴 row. Therefore a historical 壴–喜 phonetic comparison cannot be made from the inspected evidence. The packet's喜 row is preserved as MC xiX and OC *qʰ(r)əʔ without conflating columns or reconstruction systems.

The exact Unicode GetUnihanData character page for 喜 was attempted but inaccessible. The generic official Unihan lookup documentation was inspected; this does not substitute for the character-specific click-through record requested by the research instructions.

No chronology is inferred from modern glosses such as 'like/love/enjoy' or from the order of dictionary definitions. The inspected sources establish early joy/rejoicing examples but do not securely date later semantic extensions.

The cited oracle-bone witnesses are identified by corpus numbers, but the inspected sources do not give secure absolute dates for each example. The earliest attested sense therefore cannot be ranked precisely from these pages; joy/rejoicing and name uses are both reported in oracle-bone material.

Bronze 喜 is also reported for music terminology and a ritual reading written 喜(饎). The relation, if any, of that ritual use to ordinary joy is not established; it should not be presented as a semantic extension without further evidence.

The drum-and-singing interpretation is a specialist source’s reconstruction of graph motivation. Academia Sinica offers two possible explanations; neither source establishes a demonstrated chronology connecting the depicted action to the word’s senses. The inspected sources do not provide a full account of every early shape or demonstrate a specific corruption in 喜 itself.

No independently documented sound correspondence supports treating 壴 as the phonetic element in 喜. Exact local readings are available for both characters in Unihan and Baxter–Sagart tables, but the official per-character Unihan URLs and the upstream Baxter–Sagart data PDF could not be inspected; local rows are preserved as local provenance only.

Later ‘like/love/enjoy’ glosses occur in modern dictionary summaries, but the inspected historical evidence does not date or establish a semantic path from early joy to those senses. Shuowen separately records 憙 and 喜; later conflation is reported by the Taiwan variants dictionary.

Commons image descriptions establish candidate identity and rights, but the direct image fetches failed, so the glyph pixels were not visually inspected. The oracle and seal images are modern redrawings, not artifact photographs. No candidate image is available from the All Rights Reserved Academia Sinica graph-history page.

items.period: Shang oracle-script style; the file page gives a Sinica source label J11924 and note 戩45.7 合23607 but no absolute date for this individual form
items.caption: An oracle-script style form of 喜 places a branched upper shape above a rounded lower enclosure. The upper shape is analyzed as 壴, an upright drum graph, and the lower as 口; the proposed drum-and-singing motivation is an interpretation, not a meaning visible in the strokes.
items.alt: Black oracle-script style character with a tall branched upper part and a rounded lower enclosure containing a short horizontal stroke.
items.selection_reason: This redraw gives a useful visual example of an oracle-script style form alongside the reported 壴-and-口 analysis. The component interpretation and its proposed association with joy remain scholarly explanations.
items.rights: Public domain and CC0 1.0 as stated on the Wikimedia Commons file page.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; no absolute date assigned to this redraw
items.caption: A small-seal style form of 喜 has a branched upper shape above two enclosed sections. Shuowen analyzes 喜 as formed from 壴 and 口, but that lexicographic account does not independently confirm the proposed drum-and-singing motivation.
items.alt: Black small-seal style character with a branched top, a rounded middle enclosure, and a broad lower enclosure.
items.selection_reason: This distinct script-style example complements the oracle-style form and illustrates a later recorded category. The redraw does not establish a dated sequence of graphic changes.
items.rights: Public domain and CC0 1.0 as stated on the Wikimedia Commons file page; the page also notes Richard Sears source permission.

limitations.text: The drum-and-singing account is a proposed explanation of the graph’s motivation. Other interpretations have been offered, and oracle-bone examples are reported with both joy and name uses without secure dates establishing their order.
These illustrations are modern redrawings of script styles, not photographs of inscribed objects. Their script labels do not establish a dated sequence of forms.
